entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Eric of Saxe-Lauenburg (died 1522), a scion of the ducal House of Ascania, played a complex role in the ecclesiastical and political landscape of the late Holy Roman Empire, serving as Prince-Bishop of Hildesheim (as Eric II) from 1502 to 1503 and subsequently as Prince-Bishop of Münster (as Eric I) from 1508 until his death. His brief, tumultuous tenure in Hildesheim, marked by an unresolved electoral dispute and the deepening of the Hildesheim Diocesan Feud, underscored the intense jurisdictional conflicts between secular princes and ecclesiastical territories on the eve of the Reformation. His career exemplifies the challenges faced by prince-bishops caught between dynastic ambition, papal authority, and the growing power of territorial rulers.

Eric's election as Bishop of Hildesheim in 1502, following the death of Berthold II of Landsberg, was immediately contested. Although confirmed by Pope Alexander VI, the Hildesheim cathedral chapter and the city itself resisted his rule, aligning with Duke Henry the Younger of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, who sought to expand his influence over the bishopric. This opposition, exacerbated by Eric's perceived lack of political skill and his family's dynastic interests, led to his resignation in 1503 in exchange for a pension. He later secured the more stable Prince-Bishopric of Münster in 1508, where he largely maintained peace, though internal resistance to his financial policies periodically surfaced. His rule in Münster, however, was less impactful than the disputes that defined his time in Hildesheim.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Eric of Saxe-Lauenburg's contested tenure in Hildesheim and his later rule in Münster illustrate the complex power struggles between secular and ecclesiastical authorities on the eve of the Reformation, contributing to regional instability and the eventual weakening of episcopal independence.
